title: microbatch-evict-prefetch-heuristics-field-report
content:
Field report: microbatch eviction + prefetch heuristics
Owner: Priya Nair (eng-serving-runtime)
Context and why this matters
- We continue to see narrow but painful p99 spikes on CPU-backed control-plane traces during high-concurrency microburst workloads. Many of our previous notes focus on batch-formation windows and timeout arithmetic; this doc isolates two related but under-explored knobs: eviction heuristics (when to drop/flush items in a forming batch) and prefetch watermarks (when to warm KV cache / tensor prefetch for expected members). Goal: find low-risk, low-cost heuristics that reduce tail latency without materially increasing token cost or harming fairness.

Testbed & config (short)
- Cluster: dedicated qual cluster (4xA5000 per node) with p99 traffic replay harness (mix of short chat, long-completion, and streaming).
- Load generator: gamma-arrival distribution, mean qps 600, 2k concurrent clients for microburst phase.
- Runtime: serving v0.36.2 branch with experimental eviction hook and prefetch GC opt-in.
- Instrumentation: full tracing (x-request-id), per-request stack sampling (1/100), NVTX around kernel launches, and flamegraphs from perf + eBPF for CPU paths.
- Metrics reported: admission latency, batch assembly time, compute time, p50/p95/p99 total, token-cost delta.

Experiment matrix (executed in order over 11/14–11/21)
- Vars: eviction-trigger (age-ms threshold), eviction-condition (age-only | size+age | urgency-weighted), prefetch-watermark (none | low=2 item ahead | high=8 items ahead), prefetch-strategy (aggressive parallel prefetch | single-threaded serialized prefetch).
- Sweep steps: age-ms in {4, 8, 16, 32}, size threshold in {1, 4, 8}, prefetch items in {0,2,8}, strategy in {parallel, serialized}.

Representative runs & outcomes (abridged)
- Baseline (no eviction hook, prefetch none): p50 42ms, p95 210ms, p99 870ms, tokens per-second baseline; several p99s corresponded to batch assembly stalls where a very old request was blocking batch flush.
- Evict age-only 16ms: p50 44ms, p95 160ms, p99 420ms. Observed ~8% increase in compute calls due to smaller batches; token cost +1.6% overall. Tail reduced substantially because long-wait items were flushed earlier.
- Evict size+age (age 8ms, size 4): p50 40ms, p95 150ms, p99 380ms. Better than age-only in throughput-sensitive windows (fewer extra compute calls).
- Urgency-weighted eviction (urgency = 0..1, demoted items with low urgency): p50 46ms, p95 132ms, p99 220ms; tokens +3.0%. This reduced p99 the most but increased p50 slightly because aggressive demotion increases chance of small batches for urgent requests.
- Prefetch low (2 items) + serialized: p50 38ms, p95 140ms, p99 330ms. Helpful for long-completion-heavy mixes; KV cache warm-up reduced compute stall variance.
- Prefetch high (8 items) + parallel: p50 36ms, p95 130ms, p99 300ms but token cost +5.6% and increased memory pressure; observed a few OOM-autoreclaims in worst-case.
- Best combined run (urgency-weighted eviction + prefetch low serialized): p50 42ms, p95 120ms, p99 190ms, tokens +2.8%. This was the best tradeoff across tests.

Profiling notes (what the tracers showed)
- Flamegraphs: two dominant stacks correlated with p99 events: (1) batch-assembly wait path where worker waits on a condition var while holding small temporary allocation; (2) KV-cache miss + scheduler wakeup sequence where prefetch could have avoided a blocking memcpy on CPU path.
- eBPF sampling: kernel scheduling hops spiked right before p99 events, indicating contention when many prefetch threads launch simultaneously.
- NVTX+CUDA: compute kernel times were stable; tail was almost entirely assembly + memory-copy contention, not GPU compute.

Observations & hypotheses
- Hypothesis A: long-standing requests that fall behind (early arrival, long-runner or blocked RPCs) are a major root cause for p99; simple age-based eviction helps but can increase compute calls.
- Hypothesis B: prefetching the KV/tensors for the next few expected items reduces CPU-side memcpy stalls and avoids wake/sleep jitter—benefit saturates quickly (2–4 items) and becomes harmful memory-wise beyond ~8 in our cluster.
- Hypothesis C: running prefetches in parallel yields slightly lower average latencies but increases variance and kernel scheduling contention; serialized prefetches are safer at scale.
- Fairness tradeoff: urgency-weighted eviction requires carefully calibrated urgency scores to avoid penalizing background batch jobs. Default scoring function must be conservative.

Actions tested (config changes we rolled in to qual only)
- Implemented urgency-score gated eviction: only evict if urgency < 0.25 AND age > 8ms. Enabled decaying urgency (per-request warmup resets).
- Added serialized prefetch worker that limits concurrent prefetch threads to 2 per core; watermark default = 2 items ahead.
- Telemetry: added per-batch histogram of flush reason (timeout | size | eviction | prefetch-trigger) and per-request tag for eviction_count.

Tradeoffs and risks
- Risk: higher compute call volume increases infra cost; measured token-cost deltas to validate economics. Urgency-weighted eviction gave best p99 but higher token delta.
- Risk: prefetch increases memory footprint and can interact poorly with multi-tenant evictions; conservative defaults are necessary.
- Risk: complexity of eligibility rules increases maintenance surface and potential for bugs that affect fairness.

Open questions / follow-ups
- How well do these heuristics generalize to CPU-backed model instances and very long-context workloads? Need separate sweep.
- Should urgency be exposed as a per-client hint in the API (customers set priority)? What semantics/cost implications?
- Can we autotune age thresholds via short continual calibration job (lightweight RL or bandit)? Prototyping note: simple hill-climb reduced p99 on a small cluster but exploration noise is high.
- Can we detect microburst onset and temporarily relax prefetch parallelism to avoid kernel contention? Explore local backoff signals (sched_wait_count).

Next steps (short list)
- Stabilize urgency-weighted eviction in staging, add e2e test that simulates mixed-urgency traffic (due 2026-02-25).
- Add a conservative prefetch limiter mode that caps memory usage per node (due 2026-03-05).
- Run CPU-model and long-context sweeps (owner: Ethan, ETA 2026-03-12).
- Put a small A/B in production on a non-critical region for 1 week with detailed telemetry (owner: Sofia).

Notes to self / TODOs
- Add reproduction script and dataset snapshot into PR (can't rely on gamma-arrival harness alone).
- Add example of urgency calculation to docs and a CLI tool to simulate demotion effects.
- Link the telemetry dashboards to console rollout so SREs can toggle heuristics per-pool.

Slack crumbs and related links
- See slack thread #serving-runtime: "prefetch spikes on staging" (Nov 10) for early traces.
- PR to review: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/842 (eviction + prefetch prototype).

Conclusion (one-liner)
- Serialized low-watermark prefetch + conservative urgency-weighted eviction reduces tail substantially with acceptable token-cost tradeoffs; conservative defaults look safe to roll to staging for longer validation.

Attachments and raw outputs (on-drive)
- perf-flame-p99-20251114.svg (raw flamegraph), nvprof-trace-20251115.log, synthetic-harness-config.yaml
